content.value: Linux is an open-source operating system kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991. Unlike Windows or macOS, Linux is free, highly customizable, and powers the vast majority of the world's servers, cloud infrastructure, and DevOps tooling.

When people say "Linux", they usually mean a **Linux distribution** (distro) — a complete OS built on the Linux kernel. Popular distros include Ubuntu, CentOS, Alpine, and Debian. In DevOps, you'll encounter Alpine (lightweight containers) and Ubuntu (general-purpose servers) most often.

content.title: Linux Architecture Layers
content.value:
graph TB
    A["👤 User Applications"] --> B["🐚 Shell (bash / zsh)"]
    B --> C["📚 System Libraries (glibc)"]
    C --> D["🧠 Linux Kernel"]
    D --> E["💻 Hardware (CPU, RAM, Disk, Network)"]
    style A fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style B fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style C fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style D fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style E fill:#1a2332,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#e2e8f0
Over 96% of the world's top 1 million servers run Linux. Every major cloud provider (AWS, GCP, Azure) defaults to Linux instances. Knowing Linux is non-negotiable for DevOps.

Think of Linux like a restaurant kitchen. The **Kernel** is the head chef who manages all the equipment (hardware). The **Shell** is the waiter who takes your orders (commands) and delivers them to the kitchen. **Applications** are the meals — the things you actually interact with.

quiz.question: What percentage of top servers run Linux?
quiz.explanation: Over 96% of the world's top 1 million servers run Linux, making it the dominant server operating system.

content.value: Linux organizes everything as files in a tree structure starting from the root directory `/`. Unlike Windows drive letters (C:, D:), Linux has a single unified tree. Think of it like a library — the root `/` is the front door, and every book (file) has a unique shelf address (path).

    ROOT["/"] --> HOME["/home"]
    ROOT --> ETC["/etc"]

    ROOT --> TMP["/tmp"]
    ROOT --> USR["/usr"]

    ROOT --> OPT["/opt"]

    HOME --> DEPLOY["/home/deploy"]

    ETC --> NGINX["/etc/nginx"]

content.title: Key Directories Cheat Sheet
content.value:
/          Root of the entire filesystem
/home      User home directories (your personal space)
/etc       Configuration files (nginx.conf, ssh settings)
/var       Variable data (logs, databases, caches)
/tmp       Temporary files (auto-cleared on reboot)
/usr       User programs and utilities
/bin       Essential command binaries (ls, cp, mv)
/opt       Optional/third-party software
/proc      Virtual filesystem exposing kernel & process info
/dev       Device files (disks, terminals)

content.title: Navigation Commands
content.value:
pwd                    # Print Working Directory — where am I?
ls                     # List files in current directory
ls -la                 # List ALL files (including hidden) with details
ls -lh                 # List with human-readable file sizes (KB, MB)
cd /home/student       # Change Directory to an absolute path
cd ..                  # Go up one level
cd ~                   # Go to your home directory
cd -                   # Go back to previous directory
find / -name "*.log"   # Search for files by name across the system
which python3          # Find where a command binary lives
Use Tab for auto-completion. Type 'cd /ho' then press Tab — it completes to 'cd /home/'. This saves massive time and prevents typos.

quiz.question: What does the command 'cd ..' do?
quiz.explanation: 'cd ..' moves you one level up in the directory tree. '..' always refers to the parent directory.

content.value: Creating, copying, moving, and deleting files are the bread and butter of Linux administration. Imagine you're organizing a filing cabinet — these commands are how you create folders, file documents, move things around, and shred what you don't need.

content.title: Creating Files and Directories
content.value:
touch file.txt              # Create an empty file
mkdir mydir                 # Create a directory
mkdir -p a/b/c              # Create nested directories in one shot
echo 'Hello' > file.txt     # Write text to a file (overwrites)
echo 'World' >> file.txt    # Append text to a file

content.title: Copying, Moving, and Deleting
content.value:
cp file.txt backup.txt      # Copy a file
cp -r dir1 dir2             # Copy a directory recursively
mv old.txt new.txt          # Rename a file
mv file.txt /tmp/           # Move a file to another location
rm file.txt                 # Delete a file
rm -r mydir                 # Delete a directory and its contents
rm -rf mydir                # Force delete without prompts

rm -rf is extremely dangerous — it deletes everything without asking. In interviews, always mention that you would use 'rm -i' (interactive) or double-check paths before running destructive commands. This shows production awareness.

content.title: Reading Files
content.value:
cat file.txt                # Print entire file content
head -n 5 file.txt          # Print first 5 lines
tail -n 5 file.txt          # Print last 5 lines
tail -f /var/log/syslog     # Follow a log file in real-time
less file.txt               # Paginated file viewer (q to quit)
wc -l file.txt              # Count lines in a file
stat file.txt               # Show file size, permissions, timestamps

quiz.question: What is the difference between '>' and '>>' in bash?
options: No difference, both write to files
'>' overwrites the file, '>>' appends to it
'>' appends to the file, '>>' overwrites it
'>' is for files, '>>' is for directories
quiz.explanation: '>' (redirect) overwrites the entire file with new content. '>>' (append) adds new content to the end of the file without removing existing content.

content.value: Linux uses a permission system to control who can read, write, or execute files. Every file has three permission groups: **owner** (u), **group** (g), and **others** (o). Think of it like a house — the owner has the master key, family members (group) have limited access, and strangers (others) may only ring the doorbell.

content.title: Linux Permission Model
content.value:
graph LR
    F["📄 File"] --> O["👤 Owner (u)\nrwx = 7"]
    F --> G["👥 Group (g)\nr-x = 5"]
    F --> OT["🌍 Others (o)\nr-- = 4"]
    O --> R1["Read (4)"]
    O --> W1["Write (2)"]
    O --> X1["Execute (1)"]
    style F fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style O fill:#162231,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style G fill:#162231,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style OT fill:#162231,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Reading Permission Strings
content.value:
-rwxr-xr--  1  student  devops  4096  Jan 1 12:00  script.sh
 │││ │││└┘└── Others: r-- (read only)
 │││ └┘└──── Group:  r-x (read + execute)
 └┘└────── Owner:  rwx (read + write + execute)
 └──────── File type: - (file) or d (directory)

content.title: Changing Permissions
content.value:
chmod +x script.sh          # Add execute permission for all
chmod 755 script.sh         # Owner: rwx, Group: r-x, Others: r-x
chmod 644 config.txt        # Owner: rw-, Group: r--, Others: r--
chmod 600 secret.key        # Owner: rw-, nobody else can access
chown student:devops file   # Change owner and group
chown -R deploy:www /var/www  # Recursively change ownership
The numeric system: r=4, w=2, x=1. Add them up per group. So 755 means owner=7(rwx), group=5(r-x), others=5(r-x). This is asked in almost every DevOps interview.

quiz.question: What does chmod 644 mean?
options: Owner can read/write, group and others can read only
Owner can read/write/execute, others have no access
Only the owner can access the file
quiz.explanation: 644 = Owner: 6 (rw-), Group: 4 (r--), Others: 4 (r--). The owner can read and write, everyone else can only read.

content.value: Every running program in Linux is a **process** with a unique Process ID (PID). Understanding processes is essential for debugging servers, managing resources, and troubleshooting in production. Think of processes like employees in an office — each has an ID badge (PID), some work in the foreground (on your screen), and some work in the background.

content.title: Process Lifecycle
content.value:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Created: fork() / exec()
    Created --> Running: Scheduler assigns CPU
    Running --> Sleeping: Waiting for I/O
    Sleeping --> Running: I/O complete
    Running --> Stopped: SIGSTOP / Ctrl+Z
    Stopped --> Running: SIGCONT / fg
    Running --> Zombie: Process exits
    Zombie --> [*]: Parent reads exit code

content.title: Viewing Processes
content.value:
ps aux                      # List all running processes
ps aux | grep nginx         # Find a specific process
top                         # Real-time process monitor
htop                        # Better interactive process monitor
pstree                      # Show process hierarchy as a tree

content.title: Managing Processes
content.value:
kill 1234                   # Send SIGTERM to PID 1234 (graceful)
kill -9 1234                # Send SIGKILL (force kill — last resort)
killall nginx               # Kill all processes named 'nginx'
nohup ./server.sh &         # Run in background, survives logout
jobs                        # List background jobs
fg %1                       # Bring job 1 to foreground
bg %1                       # Resume job 1 in background

Interview tip: Always explain that you'd try 'kill' (SIGTERM) before 'kill -9' (SIGKILL). SIGTERM lets the process clean up gracefully (save data, close connections). SIGKILL is a last resort that can leave corrupted files. This shows production maturity.

quiz.question: What is the difference between kill and kill -9?
options: kill sends SIGTERM (graceful), kill -9 sends SIGKILL (force)
kill works on files, kill -9 works on processes
quiz.explanation: 'kill' sends SIGTERM which asks the process to shut down gracefully (save state, close connections). 'kill -9' sends SIGKILL which immediately terminates the process with no cleanup.

content.value: Pipes and redirection are the secret superpowers of Linux. They let you **chain commands together** like an assembly line in a factory — the output of one command becomes the input of the next. This is how you build powerful one-liners that process data instantly.

content.title: How Pipes Work
content.value:
graph LR
    A["cat server.log"] -->|pipe| B["grep ERROR"]
    B -->|pipe| C["sort"]
    C -->|pipe| D["uniq -c"]
    D -->|pipe| E["head -10"]
    E --> F["📊 Top 10 Errors"]
    style A fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style B fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style C fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style D fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style E fill:#1a2332,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#e2e8f0
    style F fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Pipe Examples (The | Symbol)
content.value:
# Count how many processes are running
ps aux | wc -l

# Find all lines containing 'error' in a log file
cat /var/log/syslog | grep -i error

# Sort files by size in human-readable format
ls -lhS /var/log/ | head -10

# Count unique IP addresses hitting your web server
cat access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10

# Chain 3 commands: find large files, sort by size, show top 5
du -ah /var | sort -rh | head -5

content.title: Redirection (>, >>, 2>, &>)
content.value:
echo 'Hello' > output.txt         # Write stdout to file (overwrite)
echo 'World' >> output.txt        # Append stdout to file
command 2> error.log              # Redirect stderr (errors) to file
command &> all.log                # Redirect BOTH stdout AND stderr
command > output.txt 2>&1         # Same thing, older syntax
command < input.txt               # Use file as stdin input
cat /dev/null > huge.log          # Fastest way to empty a file
The pipe symbol (|) passes the STDOUT of the left command as STDIN to the right command. Think of it like connecting two hoses — water flows from left to right.

quiz.question: What does 'ps aux | grep nginx | wc -l' do?
options: Lists all processes, filters for nginx, then counts the matching lines
quiz.explanation: The pipe chain: ps aux lists all processes → grep nginx filters for lines containing 'nginx' → wc -l counts those lines. This gives you the number of nginx processes running.

content.value: Linux has incredibly powerful built-in tools for searching, filtering, and transforming text. These three commands — **grep**, **sed**, and **awk** — are the Swiss Army knives of DevOps. They let you parse log files, extract data, and automate text manipulation instantly.

content.title: Text Processing Toolkit
content.value:
graph TD
    INPUT["📄 Raw Text / Log File"] --> GREP["🔍 grep\nSearch & Filter lines"]
    INPUT --> SED["✏️ sed\nFind & Replace text"]
    INPUT --> AWK["📊 awk\nExtract columns & compute"]
    GREP --> OUTPUT["📋 Processed Output"]
    SED --> OUTPUT
    AWK --> OUTPUT
    style INPUT fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style GREP fill:#162231,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style SED fill:#162231,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style AWK fill:#162231,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style OUTPUT fill:#1a2332,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: grep — Search for Patterns
content.value:
grep 'error' server.log           # Find lines containing 'error'
grep -i 'error' server.log        # Case-insensitive search
grep -r 'TODO' /src/              # Recursively search entire directory
grep -n 'panic' app.log           # Show line numbers with results
grep -c 'warning' server.log      # Count matching lines
grep -v 'debug' server.log        # Show lines NOT matching (invert)
grep -E 'error|warning|critical' server.log  # Search multiple patterns (regex)

content.title: sed — Stream Editor (Find & Replace)
content.value:
# Replace first occurrence on each line
sed 's/old/new/' file.txt

# Replace ALL occurrences (global flag)
sed 's/http/https/g' config.txt

# Delete lines containing a pattern
sed '/debug/d' server.log

# Edit file in-place (careful!)
sed -i 's/localhost/0.0.0.0/g' config.yaml

# Print only lines 10-20
sed -n '10,20p' file.txt

content.title: awk — Column Extraction & Analysis
content.value:
# Print the first column (space-separated)
awk '{print $1}' file.txt

# Print specific columns from /etc/passwd
awk -F: '{print $1, $6}' /etc/passwd      # Username and home dir

# Sum numbers in column 3
awk '{sum += $3} END {print sum}' data.txt

# Find lines where column 5 > 1000 (e.g., large file sizes)
ls -l | awk '$5 > 1000 {print $9, $5}'

# Count unique HTTP status codes from access.log
awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Interview combo: 'How would you find the top 10 IP addresses in an access log?' Answer: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10. This one-liner is asked in almost every DevOps interview!

quiz.question: What does 'grep -r "TODO" /src/' do?
options: Recursively searches all files under /src/ for lines containing 'TODO'
quiz.explanation: grep -r performs a recursive search through all files and subdirectories under /src/, printing every line that contains the text 'TODO'.

content.value: Cron is the Linux task scheduler — it lets you run commands automatically at specific times or intervals. Think of it like setting an alarm clock for your server: 'Every day at 2 AM, clean up old log files' or 'Every 5 minutes, check if the web server is healthy.'

content.title: Cron Expression Format
content.value:
graph LR
    A["┌─ Minute (0-59)"] --> B["┌─ Hour (0-23)"]
    B --> C["┌─ Day of Month (1-31)"]
    C --> D["┌─ Month (1-12)"]
    D --> E["┌─ Day of Week (0-7)"]
    E --> F["Command to Run"]
    style A fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style B fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style C fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style D fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style E fill:#1a2332,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#e2e8f0
    style F fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Cron Expression Examples
content.value:
# ┌───── minute (0-59)
# │ ┌───── hour (0-23)
# │ │ ┌───── day of month (1-31)
# │ │ │ ┌───── month (1-12)
# │ │ │ │ ┌───── day of week (0=Sun, 7=Sun)
# │ │ │ │ │
# * * * * *  command

  0 2 * * *   /scripts/backup.sh          # Every day at 2:00 AM
 */5 * * * *   /scripts/healthcheck.sh     # Every 5 minutes
  0 0 * * 0   /scripts/weekly-cleanup.sh  # Every Sunday at midnight
  0 9 1 * *   /scripts/monthly-report.sh  # 1st of every month at 9 AM
 30 8 * * 1-5 /scripts/morning-alert.sh   # Mon-Fri at 8:30 AM

content.title: Managing Cron Jobs
content.value:
crontab -e                 # Edit your cron jobs (opens editor)
crontab -l                 # List all your scheduled jobs
crontab -r                 # Remove ALL your cron jobs (careful!)
sudo crontab -u deploy -l  # View another user's cron jobs

# System-wide cron directories:
ls /etc/cron.daily/        # Scripts run once daily
ls /etc/cron.hourly/       # Scripts run once hourly
ls /etc/cron.weekly/       # Scripts run once weekly

Common cron gotcha: Cron runs with a minimal environment — it doesn't load your .bashrc or .profile. Always use full paths in cron jobs (e.g., /usr/bin/python3 instead of python3). This catches many people in production!

Interview tip: 'How would you schedule a log rotation every night at 2 AM?' Answer: Add '0 2 * * * /usr/sbin/logrotate /etc/logrotate.conf' to your crontab with 'crontab -e'. Also mention that most production systems use logrotate with a daily cron already configured.

quiz.question: What does the cron expression '*/5 * * * *' mean?
options: Run on the 5th of every month
quiz.explanation: '*/5' in the minute field means 'every 5 minutes'. The asterisks in the remaining fields mean 'every hour, every day, every month, every day of the week'.
